WASHINGTON (CNN) -- As he walks past the tiny, dingy waiting area into an equally cramped garage, Nui Srisook says business at his car repair shop is thriving. Drivers are choosing to keep their old cars longer, and they're turning to repair shops to make it so, observers say. Sales are up 20 percent this month and Srisook spends most nights working late, helping his customers to get extra mileage out of their old cars. "Most of the customers right now we see, they don't really have much extra money to ... buy a new car. So that's why they just do repair," Srisook said. "And now, people are willing to spend more money on maintaining the car, deciding what is broke, anything that needs to be maintained on the car." As more cash-strapped Americans turn to do-it-yourself projects and bargain shopping, car repair shops like Srisook's are feeling the boon. Drivers are choosing to keep their old cars longer, and often they're willing to put in the money to do so, observers say. The Automotive Service Association reports their members' sales were up 16 percent over last year.  Watch Kate Bolduan's report on the thriving auto repair industry » . "That indicated that people were coming in and putting the vehicle in the repair facilities' hands and saying, 'Look, I am going to be keeping this car. I want to be sure it runs well. I want to be sure that if there are any safety issues or any maintenance issues that I have overlooked, let's get those taken care of,' " said ASA President Ron Pyle. Pyle said that's a change from the past, when drivers would scrimp on the cost of maintenance and repair. "That was surprising news. We didn't expect that in the midst of the beginnings of the economic woes," Pyle said. "But they are looking at the cost of trying to purchase a new vehicle ... so I think that in relative terms that $1,000 repair to keep a $2,500 car running may be an attractive alternative." The economic slump has cut automakers deeply. Last month, sales of new cars were down more than 40 percent compared with the same time last year, according to sales tracker Autodata. The trend seems to have translated into increased traffic at auto parts stores. "We're doing way more business. The phones are ringing, you know, customers are walking in," said Darryl Wright, owner of D.C. Brake & Bearings Co. "Basically, if it's broke, they fix it." In the past, only savvy auto mechanics knew to shop at Wright's nondescript discount store. Now, he sees more car owners who are looking for a cheaper deal on parts. "[Customers will] find a guy on the street, you know -- Joe Shady Mechanics is what we call them -- to fix it at a deeper discount rate, labor-wise, and they'll send the customer in here to buy the parts on their own," Wright said. "So people are saving money that way too." Srisook said he keeps service prices low to appeal to those bargain shoppers, such as Esther White, a loyal customer. She brought in her daughter's 1996 Oldsmobile for new rotors and brakes, and said her daughter would be driving the car "until it drops dead." "Believe it or not, we were raised to fix things, and to hold on to things as long as we could," White said. "But it goes back to today's economy, and making the right financial decisions."

**Title:** Driven to Extend: How Economic Pressures Are Fueling a Boom in Auto Repairs

In an era defined by persistent inflation, high interest rates, and soaring living expenses, the traditional American rite of passage—upgrading to a shiny new car every few years—is rapidly becoming a luxury of the past. Facing sticker shock at dealership lots and prohibitive monthly loan payments, cash-strapped drivers are rethinking their approach to transportation. Rather than taking on debt for a new or late-model used vehicle, millions of consumers are making a pragmatic pivot: they are choosing to hold onto their current vehicles for as long as possible.

This shift in consumer behavior is transforming how people view auto care. Major engine overhauls, transmission rebuilds, and comprehensive suspension work, which were once viewed as indicators that a car was nearing the end of its life, are now seen as smart, cost-effective investments. Drivers are increasingly willing to drop thousands of dollars on heavy maintenance and professional repairs, recognizing that fixing an old vehicle is vastly cheaper than absorbing the steep depreciation and financing costs associated with a replacement. Consequently, the average age of cars on the road has climbed to record highs, with many vehicles routinely topping 150,000 to 200,000 miles.

This strategic emphasis on vehicle preservation has triggered an unprecedented windfall for the automotive repair sector. Independent mechanics, dealership service departments, and auto parts retailers are experiencing a significant surge in sales and foot traffic. Garages across the country report packed schedules, with appointment backlogs extending weeks into the future. From routine preventative maintenance—like regular oil changes and brake replacements—to complex diagnostic and mechanical work, service providers are seeing robust demand across the board.

However, this boom is not without its challenges. The influx of older, more complex repair jobs has placed a strain on the industry’s workforce, highlighting a growing shortage of skilled automotive technicians. Additionally, supply chains are working double-time to keep up with the demand for replacement parts for models that, in previous decades, would have already been sent to the scrapyard. 

Ultimately, the trend toward extending vehicle lifespans represents a broader economic coping mechanism. In a tight financial climate, practical necessity is overriding the desire for the latest technology and sleek designs. As long as economic hardships linger and the cost of buying a vehicle remains elevated, the strategy of prioritizing repair over replacement will continue to dictate consumer habits, keeping local garages busy and aging cars reliably on the road.

counterfactuals.output:
**Headline:** Sticker Shock at the Dealership is Driving a Boom at the Repair Shop
**Byline:** Gabe Cohen, CNN Business
**Dateline:** CHICAGO (CNN) — 

Inside a sprawling auto repair bay on Chicago’s North Side, the air is thick with the scent of motor oil and the deafening whine of pneumatic wrenches. Every hoist is occupied, and the parking lot outside is packed bumper-to-bumper.

For shop owner Marco Garcia, business hasn't just been good—it’s been overwhelming. 

"Two years ago, people would look at a $2,000 engine repair and say, 'Forget it, I’ll just trade it in,'" Garcia says, wiping grease from his hands. "Now? They’re paying for the repair before I even finish writing the estimate. They aren't looking for a new car anymore. They just want to keep the one they have alive."

As persistent inflation, high interest rates, and elevated sticker prices continue to squeeze American wallets, a distinct shift is taking place on the nation’s highways. Driven away from dealership showrooms by economic uncertainty, consumers are choosing to patch up their aging vehicles rather than take on massive new debt. 

The result is a golden age for the auto repair industry—and a stark reminder of the financial pressure hitting middle-class households.

### **The 12.5-Year Itch**

According to new data from S&P Global Mobility, the average age of passenger cars on U.S. roads has hit a record high of 12.5 years. For light trucks and SUVs, the numbers are similarly elevated. 

It’s a trend born of necessity. While the supply chain bottlenecks that plagued the auto industry during the pandemic have largely resolved, prices never truly came back down to earth. 

> **BY THE NUMBERS: THE CAR SQUEEZE**
> * **$47,870:** Average price of a new car in the U.S. (Source: Kelley Blue Book)
> * **9.6%:** Average interest rate on a used car loan.
> * **12.5 years:** Record-high average age of vehicles on American roads.

"We are seeing a perfect storm of affordability issues," says Jessica Caldwell, chief analyst at Edmunds. "When you combine high vehicle prices with interest rates pushing average monthly payments past $700, consumers are making a rational economic choice. Dropping $1,500 on a transmission repair hurts, but it pales in comparison to taking on a five-year, multi-thousand-dollar liability."

### **Choosing the 'Lesser of Two Evils'**

For Sarah Lin, a high school teacher and mother of two, the math was simple. Standing in the lobby of Garcia’s garage, she was waiting to pick up her 2011 Honda Pilot, which had just undergone $1,800 worth of suspension and brake work.

"My husband and I went to a dealership last month just to look," Lin said. "The monthly payment they quoted us for a basic crossover was more than our first apartment's rent. It was sickening. Spending two grand to keep this car running another year or two is the lesser of two evils."

Lin is far from alone. Auto parts retailers and independent repair networks are reporting record revenues. Shares of major aftermarket parts suppliers like AutoZone and O’Reilly Auto Parts have surged as Wall Street bets on the longevity of the average American vehicle.

### **A Crossroads for the Auto Industry**

While independent mechanics thrive, the trend poses a growing problem for major automakers and dealerships, who are watching inventory pile up on lots. To move metal, some manufacturers have begun reintroducing incentives and zero-percent financing promotions, but analysts say it may not be enough to break the psychological barrier for cautious consumers.

Back at the Chicago garage, Marco Garcia walks down a line of sedans and SUVs, pointing out odometers with 150,000, 180,000, and even 230,000 miles. 

"Cars are built better today than they were twenty years ago, so they can handle this kind of mileage," Garcia says. "As long as the economy stays where it is, my phone is going to keep ringing off the hook."

For millions of Americans navigating an uncertain financial landscape, the message is clear: the most affordable car on the market right now is the one already sitting in their driveway.

**CLUNKERS OVER SHOWROOMS: As New Car Sales Tank 40%, Local Mechanics and Discount Parts Stores See Recession Boom**

**CLEVELAND — October 14, 2009** — On the slick glass floor of Metro Ford, just off the highway, the silence is deafening. Brightly polished 2009 sedans sit beneath fluorescent lights, untouched by buyers whose lines of credit have dried up alongside their economic confidence. 

Three miles down the road, at Sal’s Auto Repair, the scene couldn’t be more different. The air is thick with the smell of motor oil and exhaust fumes, punctuated by the rhythmic, deafening rattle of pneumatic impact wrenches. Cars spill out of the garage bays and line the surrounding curb, waiting for service.

As the Great Recession continues to ravage the U.S. economy, the automotive industry is experiencing a tale of two starkly different realities. Major automakers and dealerships are reeling from a historic slump, with national new vehicle sales dropping by an unprecedented 40% compared to pre-recession peaks. Yet, while Detroit’s giants flounder, neighborhood mechanics and discount auto parts retailers are riding an unprecedented economic wave. 

Driven by tight credit markets, widespread job insecurity, and shrinking household budgets, American drivers are abandoning the dream of the new car smell. Instead, they are desperate to keep their current vehicles—often dubbed "beaters"—running for just a few more miles.

### Fixing, Not Replacing

"Two years ago, if a guy came in here with a 2001 Honda Civic needing a $1,200 transmission overhaul, he’d laugh, leave the keys, and go buy a new car," said Sal Marino, owner of Sal’s Auto Repair, as he wiped grease from his hands with a red rag. "Now? He’s writing the check, asking me if I can get it to 250,000 miles, and asking for a discount on a tune-up."

Marino says his business has jumped nearly 35% in the past year alone. His shop is so backlogged that customers are waiting up to ten days just for routine maintenance. 

That shift in consumer behavior is reflected in national data. According to industry surveys, the average age of passenger cars on American roads has surged to a record high of 10.4 years. 

"Consumers are locked in a survival mindset," said Ray Pomeroy, a regional spokesperson for the Automotive Service Association (ASA), an organization representing independent automotive service professionals. "Our members across the country are seeing a dramatic surge in demand, particularly for major mechanical repairs—transmissions, engine overhauls, and timing belts. What used to be considered a 'totaled' mechanical failure is now seen by consumers as a necessary expense to avoid a $400-a-month car payment."

Pomeroy noted that while independent repair shops are thriving, the shift has forced mechanics to adapt. "Shop owners are working with customers on payment plans, offering used or refurbished parts, and helping drivers prioritize safety repairs over cosmetic ones. The industry hasn't seen a shift toward preservation like this since the oil crises of the 1970s."

### The Budget-Conscious Driver

For many Americans, keeping an old car on the road is no longer a choice—it’s a financial imperative. 

Brenda Vance, a 42-year-old administrative assistant from suburban Lakewood, brought her 2002 Ford Focus into Marino’s shop on Wednesday morning after the check engine light flickered on. Vance’s husband was laid off from his construction job earlier this year, making a new car purchase entirely out of the question.

"I used to trade in my car every four years like clockwork," Vance said, leaning against the counter in the repair shop's cramped waiting room. "Right now, my biggest fear isn’t that this car breaks down—it’s the idea of taking on new debt. If paying $600 to replace an alternator and some belts keeps us out of a dealership showroom for another two years, I consider that a massive win."

Vance isn't alone. Across the country, households are diverting funds that once went toward down payments into maintenance budgets. 

### The DIY and Discount Surge

It isn't just professional repair bays that are benefiting from the slump. Discount auto parts retailers such as AutoZone, Advance Auto Parts, and O'Reilly Auto Parts have reported record quarterly profits throughout 2008 and 2009. Wall Street has designated the sector as virtually "recession-proof."

Weekend mechanics and desperate car owners are filling the aisles of these discount chains, buying spark plugs, brake pads, and oil filters to perform maintenance themselves. 

At a local AutoZone, store manager Marcus Higgins pointed to empty shelves where car batteries and brake rotor kits usually sit. 

"People are coming in with printouts from YouTube, trying to figure out how to change their own starter motors," Higgins said. "Ten years ago, people bought air fresheners and car wax here. Today, they’re buying heavy-duty jacks and shop manuals. They want to save every nickel on labor costs."

### A Changing Automotive Landscape

The federal government attempted to jump-start the lagging new car market earlier this summer with the "Cash for Clunkers" program, which offered trade-in allowances for older, less fuel-efficient vehicles. While the program provided a brief, temporary spike in showroom foot traffic, industry analysts say it did little to alter the underlying economic reality.

With unemployment lingering near 10% nationwide, economists predict that the "repair over replace" trend will persist long after the broader economy begins to recover. 

Back at Sal’s Auto Repair, Marino hoisted another rusting sedan up on the hydraulic lift. 

"The Big Three in Detroit might be hurting, but out here on the street, the automobile isn't going anywhere," Marino said with a grin. "As long as people need to get to work, and as long as they can't afford a new ride, we’re going to keep turning wrenches."

*By CNN Staff*
*Accompanies "CNN News Central" with Kate Bolduan*

**(CNN) —** For tens of millions of Americans, the daily commute is turning into an exercise in financial survival. 

As the cost of living continues to squeeze household budgets, keeping a car on the road has never been more expensive. Between soaring auto insurance premiums, high interest rates on car loans, and shop labor rates pushing past $150 an hour, drivers are reaching a breaking point. 

Instead of handing over their keys and a credit card at the local dealership, a growing wave of Americans is turning to bargain-basement part hunting, YouTube tutorials, and driveway mechanics to keep their wheels turning.

On *CNN News Central*, anchor Kate Bolduan takes an in-depth look at how everyday drivers are adapting to the automotive affordability crisis—and how local shop owners are on the frontlines of this major consumer shift.

### "Just Make It Drive"

At independent repair shops across the country, the change in customer behavior is stark. 

Nui Srisook, owner of an independent auto repair shop, says he sees the financial strain on his customers' faces every day. Where clients used to routinely approve recommended maintenance packages, today’s drivers are prioritizing strictly what is necessary to keep the vehicle moving.

"A few years ago, people would come in and say, 'Fix whatever needs fixing,'" Srisook told CNN. "Now, the conversation is entirely different. People bring in a list of three or four issues, look at the estimate, and ask: *'Which one of these keeps the car from breaking down on the highway tomorrow?'* They are skipping the non-essentials just to get by."

Srisook noted that more customers are also asking if they can bring in their own parts—often ordered off bargain websites or bought second-hand—to cut down on the shop's markup. While it’s a strategy that can save money upfront, Srisook warns it carries risks if the parts are counterfeit or low quality, though he understands why drivers are taking the gamble.

"When money is tight, people do what they have to do," Srisook said. "They are trying to survive until the next paycheck."

### The DIY Boom—and Its Pitfalls

For those who can’t afford professional labor costs at all, the driveway has become the new garage. Sales of basic automotive tool sets, diagnostic code readers, and aftermarket parts have surged as drivers attempt tasks once left strictly to professionals—from changing brake pads and spark plugs to replacing alternators.

Darryl Wright, who owns and operates a local auto supply and service shop, has seen a dramatic uptick in first-time DIYers walking through his doors. 

"Ten years ago, the average person coming into my shop wanted an air freshener or wiper blades," Wright said. "Today, I’ve got young adults and parents coming in holding up a broken sensor or an alternator, pulling up a YouTube video on their phone, and asking, 'Can you show me which wrench opens this?'"

Wright says he applauds the resourcefulness of cash-strapped drivers, but he also spends a lot of his time offering cautionary advice. Modern vehicles are heavily computerized, and a wrong move on a complex repair can quickly turn a $200 fix into a $2,000 mistake.

"I tell people all the time: changing your oil or your air filter is a great way to save $50," Wright explained. "But when you start messing with complex electrical systems or critical safety components without the right experience, you can end up digging a much deeper hole. There’s a fine line between saving money and putting yourself in danger."

### A Middle-Class Squeeze on Wheels

The shift toward DIY repairs and bargain shopping highlights a broader economic reality. According to recent consumer price data, auto maintenance and repair costs have jumped significantly faster than overall inflation over the past three years. Combined with the average age of cars on U.S. roads hitting a record high of 12.5 years, drivers are trying to keep older, more breakdown-prone vehicles running longer than ever before.

For many, learning how to turn a wrench isn't a weekend hobby—it's an economic imperative. 

As Kate Bolduan explores in her report, the trend reflects the grit of American consumers determined to stay mobile, even as the traditional costs of car ownership slip out of reach.

***

*Watch Kate Bolduan’s full report on the rising cost of auto repairs and the DIY revolution on CNN.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a realistic news article from the perspective of a Washington journalist examining how everyday citizens are adapting to financial hardship by repairing old cars, featuring interviews with local business owners and ASA President Ron Pyle?
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON** — Every morning at 6:00 a.m., Marcus Vance turns the key of his 2011 Honda Accord and holds his breath. With 218,000 miles on the odometer, a lingering power steering whine, and a sun-faded hood, the sedan is far from pretty. 

A year ago, Vance, a facilities technician from Woodbridge, Virginia, who commutes daily into downtown Washington, would have traded it in. But when he looked at current auto loan rates—hovering around 7% for prime borrowers and well into the double digits for others—and average new car prices exceeding $47,000, he made a calculated choice. 

Instead of taking on an $800 monthly car payment, Vance spent $2,400 to replace the Accord’s clutch, timing belt, and water pump.

"It hurt to drop two grand all at once," Vance said, leaning against the counter of a local repair shop in Northeast D.C. "But that’s three months of a new car payment. If this repair gives me two more years, I win."

Vance’s story is becoming the standard narrative across the Washington metropolitan area and the nation. As sticky inflation, high interest rates, and elevated living costs continue to squeeze household budgets, everyday citizens are abandoning the dream of the new car smell. Instead, they are turning to a strategy of extreme vehicle longevity—nursing decade-old "beaters" past markers once considered terminal.

According to recent industry data, the average age of passenger cars on U.S. roads has reached a record high of 12.6 years. In working-class suburban pockets surrounding the Beltway, independent repair shops are feeling the brunt of this shift.

### "Lifts Are Always Full"

For local business owners, the economic strain on consumers has translated into a sustained surge in demand for heavy mechanical repairs.

"Five years ago, if a customer got a quote for a $3,000 transmission job on a 15-year-old car, they’d hand us the keys and walk over to the dealership," said Dave Miller, owner of Miller’s Auto Care in Silver Spring, Maryland. "Now? They say, 'How fast can you get the parts?'"

Miller says his four repair bays have been fully booked three weeks in advance for almost a year. The nature of the work has shifted dramatically, moving away from routine oil changes and tire rotations toward major engine overhauls and rust mitigation.

"People are deferring the cosmetic stuff—the broken power windows, the clear coat peeling off—and pouring every dollar they have into keeping the drivetrain reliable," Miller added. "It’s purely about survival and getting to work."

The trend is echoed across town at Capitol Beltway Auto Parts in Northeast D.C., a family-owned supplier operating since 1988. Co-owner Elena Torres noted a marked increase in demand for remanufactured and reconditioned components over brand-new OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) parts.

"Customers are asking for salvaged or rebuilt parts to keep the bill down," Torres said. "We’re selling reconditioned alternators and salvaged steering racks as fast as we can source them. The mindset has completely shifted from luxury and modern tech to basic utility."

### Industry Leadership Weighs In

The national scope of this trend is no surprise to trade leaders who monitor the health of the automotive aftermarket. 

Ron Pyle, President and CEO of the Automotive Service Association (ASA)—the national organization representing independent automotive service and repair shop owners—notes that independent shops are playing an increasingly critical role in keeping the American workforce mobile during lean economic times.

"We are seeing a fundamental shift in how consumers view auto maintenance," Pyle said in an interview. "A few years ago, the threshold for declaring a car a 'total loss' based on repair costs was much lower. Today, consumers are running the numbers. They realize that spending $2,500 or $3,000 to keep a paid-off, twelve-year-old vehicle on the road is fundamentally smarter than entering a five- to seven-year debt commitment at high interest rates."

Pyle emphasized that this surge in demand presents both opportunities and operational hurdles for independent repair facilities, which perform the vast majority of out-of-warranty vehicle repairs in the U.S.

"Our member shops are seeing unprecedented volume, but they’re also managing complex repairs on aging vehicles that require specialized diagnostic skills," Pyle noted. "The challenge for the independent shop owner isn't finding work—it's navigating supply chain delays for older parts and educating consumers on preventative maintenance so they don't end up stranded. What used to be considered a 'disposable vehicle' is now a family's primary economic lifeline."

### The Math of Staying on the Road

For commuters in the D.C. region, where public transit doesn't always bridge the gap between outer-ring suburbs and dispersed job sites, a personal vehicle remains non-negotiable. 

Economic analysts point out that while maintaining an older car comes with risks—such as unpredictable breakdowns and lower fuel efficiency—the math firmly favors repair over replacement in today's market. 

According to Bankrate, the average interest rate for a used car loan currently sits near 11.5%. On a $20,000 used car financed for 60 months, a borrower with average credit can expect to pay thousands in interest alone over the life of the loan, not including higher insurance premiums often required by lenders for newer vehicles.

Back in Silver Spring, Dave Miller hands Marcus Vance the keys to his repaired 2011 Accord. The engine starts smoothly, the clutch pedal firm underfoot. 

"She’s got another 50,000 miles in her if you treat her right," Miller tells him.

Vance smiles, slips the receipt into his glovebox—right next to the original owner's manual—and pulls out onto the asphalt of the Beltway, joining thousands of other drivers holding on to the wheels they already own.
